utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, if I may address you. This is your application, as I understand it, to exclude evidence obtained from a search executed in September of last year in Vitez by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. It may simplify matters if I briefly indicated what it appears to me are the issues in this matter. The Defence argue, on behalf of Mr. Kordic, that there was an illegal search by the Office of the Prosecutor of the premises of a Bosnian government agency and evidence was seized in violation of the rights of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you allege, Mr. Smith, the basic principles of criminal procedure. The cooperation and assistance of the Bosnian authorities was not sought as required by Bosnian law on cooperation with the Tribunal and, you said, customary international practice. A search warrant, you say, was executed without regard to the authorised scope of the search in a different location and, you say, without providing a detailed inventory and the document have not been returned. Therefore, you argue that all the documents recovered should be excluded. There seems, in fact, on the evidence to be very little dispute about what happened. Please indicate in due course what you say is in dispute. We have the affidavits of Mr. Zigonjic, the head of the defence office at Vitez, with attached exhibits; the affidavits of Mr. Tadic, the Minister of Justice of the federation; and Mr. Antunovic, the head of the defence administration in Travnik. You also ask, and I don't know whether this is being dealt with by agreement, for an inventory of everything that's been recovered during the search. The Prosecution response of the 5th of February we have, arguing that your client doesn't have the locus to challenge this, his rights not having being affected, only those of the government. They argue that the Prosecutor was entitled to carry out the investigation, Article 18(2) of the Statute saying that the Prosecutor has the power to collect evidence and in so doing she may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of state authorities. Rule 39 of the Rules allow the Prosecutor to collect evidence and undertake such other matters as appear necessary for completing the investigation and seek to that end the assistance of governments. They argue that the Prosecutor wasn't required to act only through the authorities of the federation and, accordingly, the evidence should not be excluded. The investigation, they say, was carried out in a lawful and proper manner. They say they're willing to provide a written list of the relevant documents in relation to the inventory, but they oppose a request for a full inventory. We have had their summary of evidence. Mr. Nice, if I may address you for one moment on this topic. The declarations, although it's true that they were summarised in an earlier document which you submitted, didn't reach, speaking for myself, my desk until this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They were ordered by the 17th of May, were dated the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our understanding of the order was that the summary was wanted by the 17th. The summary was provided and the detailed documents were provided later. They were certainly filed last week and I'm sorry they didn't reach your desk until today, but that was our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Smith, it's for you to begin. As I say, we've had these papers, and I would invite you to deal with the matter as expeditiously as you feel able. Having regard to this fact, I believe there's a witness here, and if there is, we would be anxious to get on with the evidence as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This request, this motion, raises three basic issues, quite fundamental issues, I believe, particularly the first. The first issue is whether the UN Security Council has granted to the Prosecutor direct enforcement authority for armed search and seizure in sovereign states, a matter, I would suggest, of some consequence. Secondly, whether, if it has, the Prosecutor has properly exercised that authority in this case. Third, the question of locus standi but in light of the Tadic appeals decision, in our judgement that establishes standing. I will not dwell on this further until the Trial Chamber wishes to go into the matter. Let me state very briefly the relevant facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless they are particularly relevant to your submissions, we have had the chance of reading all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We should proceed directly to the argument, Your Honour. First, the question of authority. Neither the Statute, in our judgement, nor the Rules of the Tribunal grant the Prosecutor authority to take direct enforcement action in the form of armed search and seizure operations within the boundaries of a sovereign state without their consent and/or participation, and we start with the proposition that the Tribunal and the Office of the Prosecutor, as an international organisation, is a body of limited and delegated authority. We point to an ICJ 1996 advisory opinion on the use of nuclear weapons that both we and the Prosecutor have cited, which establishes an earlier decision. And speaking of the European Community, a highly developed organisation "as the European commission" -- this is a quotation: "As the European commission is not a state but an international institution with a special purpose, it has only," and I underline that word because it is in our quote but in the quotation in the Prosecutor's brief they picked up the quotation just after that word, "It only has the functions bestowed upon it by the definitive Statute with a view to the fulfilment of that purpose but it has the power to exercise those functions to their fullest extent insofar as the statue does not impose restrictions upon it." This establishes that the Tribunal is not a state and is not sovereign. It establishes that it is a body of limited and delegated authority but with fulsome right to exercise the authority delegated. In this case, by the Security Council through the Statute. Third, it is true, I believe, that in any case, as even a sovereign nation would be, both the Tribunal and the Prosecutor, however independent the Prosecutor may be, are bound to the limitations imposed by international law and that the Security Council in enacting a Statute enacts it, as does a legislature generally, against the background of applicable, binding law, in this case, international law. Insofar as the Tribunal is authorised and the Prosecutor's office is authorised to exercise their functions "to the fullest extent," that must mean to the fullest extent allowed by law, that is to say, the international law. I will not dwell on the principles of international law applicable to the use of force in search and seizure operations upon the territory of a sovereign state because that matter is dealt with at some length in our briefs. But it is clear that under international law, any entity, other than the sovereign state itself, that wishes to exercise what our essentially executive powers of sovereignty within the territory of a sovereign state must have the consent and the assistance of the sovereign state, and there are bilateral and multilateral treaties, as well as model conventions, commonwealth schemes that lay out the mutual judicial assistance provisions which apply. It is important, turning first to the question of the language of the Statute, to note in general that the Tribunal has been granted judicial authority and not executive authority, and it is also important to note that given the general international law prohibiting the exercise of armed search and seizure operations in the territory of a sovereign country, any such power granted by the Statute, the language of which we will examine in a moment, necessarily would need to be express, quite express, because it would run counter to the general thrust of international law and the rights of the member states of the UN that enacted the Statute or that authorised the Statute through the Security Council. I think it might be useful to look at what people have said about this question of the enforcement authority of the Tribunal. We have set out in our brief at page 11 statements in the first report of the ICTY, a statement by the Court in the Blaskic appellate judgement on subpoenas, statements by then President Cassese of the Tribunal, statements by President McDonald during her tenure as recently as November of 1998 after the search and seizure in question, and in our brief requesting an inventory and notice, we have also quoted the Prosecutor herself in an interview only days before this search and seizure, all of which stand directly for the proposition that they read the Statute as providing no direct enforcement authority and no authority for armed search and seizure unilaterally exercised in sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, let me stop you. Whereabouts in the brief, first of all, are we going to find these comments referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: They're on page 11 and 12, Your Honour. I had planned to read them but decided not to in light of Your Honour's injunction for brevity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just so that we have a note of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. At pages 11 and 12, footnotes 22, and then a commentator to the same effect, Mr. Fredereik Harhoff writing in the international view of the Red Cross in footnote 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You referred also to the application for an inventory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that will take me a moment because I have it in my bag. May I suggest that I proceed and ask one of my co-counsel to find that quotation in that brief, Your Honour, and we will supply you the page number in a moment. Let me turn then to Article 16, cited by the Prosecutor as a potential basis for authority. Article 16 provides that OTP is "responsible for" investigations of war crimes, but that is not a grant, it seems to me, of power in the face of the sovereign rights of countries. It further provides that the OTP shall act "independently," but that cannot mean arbitrarily or lawlessly, and this Trial Chamber must be the forum in which to judge the lawfulness of the Prosecutor's conduct under Article 95 of its Rules. Let me turn then to Article 18, which Your Honour has mentioned in his summary. This provides first in its first subsection that the OTP shall "initiate investigations" and "assess information." That does not, in our submission, constitute a direct grant of authority to engage in armed searches in a sovereign territory without consent. In Article 18, paragraph 2, we have the language authorising the Prosecutor to conduct "on-site investigations" and to "collect evidence." That, Your Honours, is as good as it gets in terms of language authorising this activity in the Statute. The Prosecutor, in briefs, argues that the activity undertaken constitutes, and they characterise it this way continuously through their brief, on-site investigation and collection of evidence. In their affidavits or in their declarations, however, they refer over and over again to the activity as one involving seizure. Thus, in the declaration by Pantz, the word "seizure" is used to characterise the activity undertaken at paragraphs 30, 32, 37, 47, 48, 49, 55, 56, and 57. Likewise, in the declaration by Dornan, the word "seizure" is used, collected and seized, in paragraph 21 and the same thing in the affidavit by Gillissen at paragraph 15. In short, Your Honours, this was not just a consensual collection of evidence and on-site investigation. This was, in fact, a coercive, inclusive search and seizure operation backed up by and expressly authorised to use armed force. What was done here was, therefore, the exercise of direct enforcement power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you leave paragraph 2 of Article 18, perhaps you can help us with the second sentence. It may be we're going to deal with it anyway, in which case I apologise, but it states that in carrying out the tasks, that is, the power to collect evidence and to conduct on-site investigations, "In carrying out these tasks, the Prosecutor may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of the State authorities concerned." Now, your argument, Mr. Smith, is that that should read "must"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would submit that it must be done, it is appropriate to be done and it must be done, not because of the language here but because of the binding international law obligations, where there is an armed search and seizure action taken, when it is that form of collecting evidence, it must be done. But there are many forms of collecting evidence where it need not be done, at least not in many countries. Now, there is a decision of the French Constitutional Court, their highest court, which is not in our brief and I brought it to the attention of the Prosecutor, in which the search and seizure provisions, the investigation provisions really, of the lone treaty involving the international criminal court were at issue, and the question was whether the French constitution had to be amended before that treaty could be ratified. The French Constitutional Court found that even in the case of a non-coercive investigation, it would violate the French constitution if the prosecutor at that point, the prosecutor of the international criminal court, were to proceed without going through the requirements under French law. I am not making that argument here because in many countries I think it might well be lawful for the prosecutor to undertake the same form of non-coercive investigation that we, as the Defence, can undertake. It is when the Prosecutor takes upon herself the attributes of sovereignty to exercise, through armed force, a search and seizure, which the Defence as private parties could never do in a country, it is at that point that we argue, not because of the may/shall language here but because of the general obligation of this Tribunal and the Prosecutor to comply with constraining international law which the Prosecutor generally ignores in their brief, as we have pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the point of putting that sentence into Article 18? If your argument is right, it's completely unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think first it alerts the Prosecutor that in many cases, it may not just be appropriate but necessary, because there are a wide range of these types of investigatory activities. So in France, it alerts the prosecutor to do even consensual activities, in effect; they must notify the French authorities. In the case of this kind of aggressive, armed search and seizure, then it alerts them that they must investigate whether they are constrained, and they are constrained to follow international legal requirements, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second sentence in Article 18(2) doesn't deal with consent, it deals with assistance which is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite correct in that, and it seems to me that it can be explained on those grounds as well. If I might go on to Article 29, Your Honour, which is related, Article 29 provides a duty to cooperate which would not be there, in our judgement, unless it were necessary. Therefore, it confirms the analysis that we make of the Statute. There would be no need for requests of cooperation, nor a duty on states to respond if the Prosecutor had free reign in conducting activities like an armed search and seizure in sovereign territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Following your argument, the logic of it is that any state that wishes to prevent the Prosecutor carrying out her duties is entitled to do so and as against such a refusal the Tribunal is powerless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, that is not the situation we face here, because there is Bosnian legislation and there is a memorandum of understanding, that I will come to in a moment, governing the assistance to be given to the Prosecutor and to the Tribunal, number one. Number two, providing a methodology similar to that employed in bilateral treaties throughout the world for judicial assistance on matters like search and seizure when armed force is required. In the first instance, I do not think we need to reach that question on these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that they should have applied to the federation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to carry out the search warrant?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the basic methodology applied in bilateral treaties on judicial assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What would happen if the entity refused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In that instance, Your Honour, the remedy for the Prosecutor and the Tribunal is to go to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What would happen to the documents, the other matters which were going to be seized meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: They might or might not stay in their original state. That's quite obvious. I concede that as a matter of fact. Nonetheless, it seems to me that what is essentially at stake in the Prosecutor's argument is whether the end justifies the means. The means have simply not been provided on the face of the Statute, other than through the exercise of national sovereignty and consent. For example, I think that if the Prosecutor attempted the same exercise in France, or the United States, or in Germany, the Prosecutor would be in some difficulty and the states involved would not think that they had granted the Tribunal or the Prosecutor the authority to engage in an armed search and seizure on their territory. With Your Honour's leave, I would move on to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The first thing to say about the Rules is they do not add to the statutory power. Rule 39 allows the Prosecutor, again, to collect evidence and conduct on-site investigations. It also allows, in (ii), the Prosecutor to "undertake such other matters as may appear necessary ..." That language, in our submission, has to mean such other matters as are authorised by Statute and as appear to be necessary because the Rules cannot expand on the statutory authority. In short then, Rule 39 does not and cannot provide the Prosecutor with more authority than the Statute does, and the Statute allows the Prosecutor to obtain a search warrant and to take it to the relevant national government to have it processed in the normal way subject to national law, as I've indicated earlier. I would turn now, Your Honour, to Bosnia and Bosnian law. Bosnia does not allow armed search and seizure operations on its sovereign territory. First, it would not matter to this case if it did. It could not grant the Prosecutor's office authority it did not already have under the Statute. Secondly, even if that were not the case, it is useful to look at several documents that we have cited and the Prosecutor has cited in briefs to see whether they provide the basis for the authority to the Tribunal or the Prosecutor to engage in an armed search on Bosnian territory without regard for Bosnian law, indeed, without advanced notice, much less advanced consent. I would start, Your Honours, with the 3 December, 1994 memorandum of understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where would we find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It is cited in our brief. I have copies with me if the court does not have access to it and would be happy to pass them out if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more convenient if you give it to us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The first thing to note, Your Honours, about the memorandum of understanding is that it is pre-Dayton. The second thing to note about it is that it is a memorandum of understanding only and it is not a treaty. This memorandum of understanding was signed by the Minister of Foreign Affairs on behalf of the government only a mere matter of months after a mixed government had been provided for. There have been efforts by both the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs to have it changed because they did not participate in its negotiation or signing. There is a new memorandum drafted and submitted but never acted on by the Bosnian government. As you know, many matters in the Bosnian government are effectively blocked if one or more of the parties objects to the action. Let me turn to the language of the memorandum of understanding itself and, in particular, first to the beginning, which states: "An agreement to cooperate fully and unconditionally with the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in the performance of his rights, duties and obligations." That language, Your Honours, provides for cooperation as required and guided under Bosnian law. Thus, any bureaucrat, under Bosnian law, who has discretion to exercise would be required to exercise that discretion so as to cooperate fully and unconditionally within his legal constraints. Secondly, I would point Your Honours to paragraph 11, which deals with documents and other investigative source material. It provides that the Prosecutor may send investigators to examine documents, et cetera, gathered by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to international potential violations of international war crimes. It provides, again, that the authorities will cooperate with such investigators and allow them access to such documents, indices, and other materials so that they can examine them, copy them, or otherwise reproduce them. It does not provide for their searching and seizing them. If original documents are required there is a provision under which investigators and the authorities make special arrangements for the original documents to be securely transmitted to The Hague. In this case, the original documents were seized and taken unilaterally to The Hague. So that, Your Honours, this paragraph, to the extent that it was intended to cover search and seizure at all, has been violated, and I suggest that it was intended to cover cooperative consensual gathering of evidence, not the unilateral armed seizure of evidence. It does not authorise that. The law that governs -- (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I'm sorry we interrupted. We were considering a matter. If you'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Paragraphs (v) and (vi) of the memorandum of understanding cited by the Prosecutor speak only of collecting evidence and on-site investigating, not armed search and seizure operations. The law that applies within Bosnia to requests from outside the country for search warrants to be executed is cited in our brief and it is the 1996 law on cooperation with the ICTY, which is subsequent to the memorandum of understanding and which is a law and thus it overrides, to the extent of any inconsistency, a prior memorandum of understanding which is not a treaty. In Article 27, which we cite, any final order to collect evidence must be executed by the Ministry of Justice and Administration in cooperation with the Interior Affairs Ministry and the Foreign Affairs Ministry. Article 6 of that law designates the code of criminal procedure of Bosnia to regulate the details of judicial assistance. The code of criminal procedure, in turn, also cited in our brief, contains Articles 518 covering requests for warrants to collect evidence which are to be submitted to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Article 519(1), which requires the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to submit such requests to a competent court, usually a court of first instance, and this is the traditional, time-honoured international law methodology for judicial assistance. It is in stark contrast, I might add, to provisions in the laws of some of -- at least one of the countries involved in the former Yugoslavia which prohibits extradition, for example. That is not this situation. This is a situation that Bosnia has provided the mechanism required by its duties under the statue. There is a similar cooperation provision in the Bosnian constitution which is to the same effect, that officials are obligated to cooperate, obviously within the bounds of legal requirements and, therefore, it governs the exercise of their discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you refer to the traditional, time-honoured international methodology for judicial assistance. Now, that time-honoured methodology deals with mutual assistance, mutual legal assistance, whatever you wish to call it, between states, inter-state. In this environment, we're not dealing with mutual legal assistance between states. The origin of this entire exercise is a resolution of the Security Council acting on the Chapter VII of United Nations's Charter, an exercise of its enforcement policy. So in my view, the analogy that you keep drawing with mutual legal assistance treaties, and which in my former career I worked for quite a long time, is really inapposite because that's a consensual basis. It must be a consensual basis as between states and you have a treaty. Here the basis of this exercise is not a treaty, it is a resolution of the United Nations, of the Security Council acting on the Chapter VII. I think there is a vast difference that you need to take up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point, and I would suggest that the procedures applicable under International Law as between sovereigns, when one sovereign attempts to exercise coercive power within the territory of another sovereign is a good guide to what the Security Council would have intended and did intend in enacting the language that we've just examined of the Statute, because the language of the Statute applies to all Member States and a holding that there is power to exercise coercive armed search and seizure in any member state of the UN created by the statute, notwithstanding this normal pattern even among sovereign states. Of course, as I started out, the United Nations and this Tribunal is not a sovereign entity. It is an international entity, as the case law in the ICJ indicates, which in the case of the UN has only the powers authorised by its charter, and in the case of this Tribunal has only the powers authorised and delegated to it under its Statute. So it seems to me the normal pattern of international law goes very strongly, at a minimum, to the intent, the likely intent of the Security Council in granting these powers, and it seems also to me that it provides an international law backdrop to the customary international law. This Tribunal is obligated to follow the rules of customary international law, and the rule of legality is a matter going to procedure as well as substance. So I would link it back into a legal obligation on the Tribunal in that regard as well, Your Honour. But your point is quite well taken about the consensual nature of those bilateral treaties. I believe, however, they reflect, in effect, customary international law. Let me then proceed with the several points that the Prosecutor makes, and I shall be brief on the authority argument now in finishing. The Prosecutor cites the primacy of the ICTY in its jurisdiction over adjudication as a bolster for its exercise of what are essentially executive, non-judicial search and seizure, armed search and seizure operations, and I suggest to you that simply to state that proposition explains why that law is inapposite. It applies to adjudication, and there is primacy there, and it does not apply to this sort of activity. They also cite the Blaskic Appeals Chamber, and I have already indicated the quotation from that Appeals Chamber that reflects directly the fact that search and seizure must be done through the use of the state activities involved, and, in any case, as our brief indicates, that case deals with witness interviews and witness protection, a different matter. The Prosecutor also cites their own Statute. We do, and they reply on that, that it is a treaty-based, consensual matter, not a matter of the Article 7 enforcement authority, but I would argue that what it provides in the way of power for search and seizure reflects the current customary international law, and it requires the consent of the affected state. It also reflects what the Security Council would have intended and did intend for the same reasons I just outlined to Your Honour. Now, the Prosecutor makes several other implicit responses in their brief in the nature of, it seems to me, that when you think you're strong on the facts, try to argue the facts. The Prosecutor says there's a great need in this situation for these powers to be possessed by the Prosecutor, and I go back to the proposition I articulated earlier in response to a question: No matter how great the need, the end cannot justify the means if the means are not granted in the Statute, and we've examined the language. Secondly, they have asserted over and over that they have acted in a polite fashion, as it were, when they undertook this investigation and that the Bosnian Croats who were searched and whose material was seized had offered them coffee. Nonetheless, Your Honours, a polite attitude by a bank robber cannot justify a bank robbery. It cannot overcome the lack of authority, and there was a threat of armed force present. There's simply no question about that. The Bosnian Croats, once they had made a decision that blood should not be spilled on this question, not withstanding sovereignty, proved that they are not nearly as obstructive as the declarations of the Prosecutor's witness indicated. There are several other things that the Prosecutor has argued, that there's been no objection by the Bosnian government officials. Well, they've got the cart before the horse. What is involved here is a violation of the rights of Bosnia in which consent was required. There has been no consent. The fact that there is not an objection lodged since then in any official manner is irrelevant to the question of whether the needed consent was obtained. As I'm sure Your Honours recognise and, I suspect, the Prosecutor recognised in engaging in the search without advance notice, that government tends to be deadlocked on issues that divide the communities. The Prosecutor stresses that what are seized are government documents, not personal documents, but that simply makes the insult to sovereignty, as we've said in our brief, that much more significant. These were not just government documents; these were national security documents. In addition, there were social security documents and pension documents that bear on the rights of individuals. Finally, the Prosecutor has argued that the Bosnian Croats, in general, have not cooperated in making material available to the Tribunal and that that somehow justifies this operation. The first thing that I would say is that it is important to focus on the fact that this is a case involving two individuals, not the Bosnian Croats generally. Secondly, the examples of lack of cooperation cited by the Prosecutor involve only one before the date of the search. Three of the ones that have been cited involve a time period after the search and really are not logically relevant to the situation facing the Prosecutor at the time of the search. Finally, we were just aware of the nature and thrust of this argument last Friday when we got the declarations by the Prosecutor. The declarations concerning the lack of cooperation went beyond the summary of evidence, and when we examined them, we undertook an investigation as to the nature of prior cooperation because this is obviously a matter that's been going on between the Prosecutor, the Tribunal, and the Bosnian government. What we found when we investigated the matter was, and we just got this information today and I called my learned colleague and informed him about it, and he's been very helpful in the further investigation of it apparently at some time earlier than the search was executed, and I believe probably in 1997, the Prosecutor at one point sent a representative to the then Minister of Defence in Bosnia, Mr. Ante Jelavic, requesting to see the archives of the HVO, which, of course, at that time after Dayton had become officially the archives of the Bosnian Federation. Mr. Jelavic issued an order authorising that and sent the Prosecutor's people with that order down to, I believe, Grude to examine those records. They found those records in Grude. They were apparently quite voluminous, and the Prosecutor's personnel apparently took the position that the Bosnians should provide the specific information requested, rather than making the material available to them on-site, and left. That set of events was apparently captured in a letter by Mr. Jelavic to Mr. Blewitt, which I did not have today but the Prosecution has been kind enough to provide to me, I have only one copy, but it is a letter which recites essentially these facts. The Prosecutor may know more facts about this. All I know at this point is the information that we were able to determine over the weekend and what I find in this letter. But apparently, as the letter says, the Minister was informed "that for reasons unknown to me, Silvie Pantz did not want to, that is, refused to examine the available files and did not allow other authorised officials from your office to have access to them either." Now, I don't fully understand and know the facts of this situation, but it does seem to me that at a minimum, the assertion in Ms. Pantz's declaration, in paragraph 4, that many requests, including some from 1997 and early 1998, have been completely ignored and stonewalled by the Bosnian Croats who have provided no assistance whatsoever, represents something of an overstatement. To conclude on the question of authority, Your Honours, what is at issue here is quite simple. First, the Prosecutor must not act unlawfully and, in our judgement, did. Second, the ends cannot justify the means if the authority to engage in the particular acts in question, armed search and seizure on the sovereign territory of a state, have not been provided by the Security Council in the Statute to the Prosecutor. Third, and I think this is quite important, Bosnia, if it is to develop as a full-fledged, well-run, internationally recognised state, it is that already, but if it is to develop and fulfil its potential, cannot be treated as a UN protectorate of some sort. Its sovereignty must be respected. If the UN expects the people in the country to take the country seriously, the UN must do so as well. Finally, to hold otherwise than to strike the evidence from this illegal search, we submit, would send entirely the wrong message to the world about the Prosecutor, the nature of the Prosecutor's allowed operations, and the nature of the Bosnian entity and state itself. I would turn now, Your Honour, briefly to the questions of the execution of the search warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Before going on to that particular issue, Mr. Smith, there's a question I would like to put to you. At this point of your arguments, you have shown that you were taking as a basis the need of the obligation for our Tribunal to respect state of sovereignty, and you referred us to the Statute, you referred us to the Rules also, and you have also recognised, however, that the Tribunal was founded on the basis of Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, a chapter which grants the Security Council the power to take binding decisions, binding on all member nations of the United Nations, as you well know, and even non-member states have to comply with the Security Council's decisions. Then as far as sovereignty is concerned, I would simply like to ask you or, rather, tell you and see how you react to it, tell you that you have overlooked Article 2, paragraph 7, of the United Nations Charter, a very important paragraph as it guarantees the international authority of states. This is what we call an exception to jurisdiction. The United Nations is an international organisation. That's a fact. It's not a sovereign organisation, it's not a superstate, as the ICJ recognises itself and you have reminded us of that particular fact in your brief, it was in 1949, I think, but the United Nations has to try not to go into matters which are directly relevant to a state and to its national jurisdiction. The article quotes in English, and I'll give it to you in English because that's all I have, and I won't do that again, but for once, I will speak in English in order to quote the text right: "... in the present Charter shall authorise the United Nations to intervene in matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state or shall also require the members to submit such matters to settle under the present Charter, but this principle shall not prejudice the application of enforcement measures under Chapter VII." That means that this particular paragraph on national jurisdiction is recognised by the Charter, with the exception that is said very clearly in Article 2, paragraph 7, an article which governs the very principles on which the United Nations rests, with the exception of the article of Chapter VII. So the argument of national sovereignty does not resist what is said in Article 2(7). In 1997, we are yet again arguing about Chapter VII as the SFOR who has taken action pursuant to Article 2(7) through a decision of the Security Council which was taken after the Dayton Agreement. Let me remind you that the Dayton Agreement had to be made legitimate by a decision of the Security Council. May I also remind you of what Article 103 of the Charter says? It's a very interesting article because you have reminded us of an agreement which was concluded between the United Nations and a member state or an agreement that is ratified by two different states. Article 103 of the Charter deals with the supreme character of the Charter. It says: "... of the members of the United Nations under the present Charter and their obligations under the international agreement, their obligations under the present Charter shall prevail." That's a crucial article, needless to say, because what does it mean? It means that whatever the agreements reached between states, there is the supremacy of the Charter over any international agreement concluded after the Charter has been adopted. That there is an obligation to cooperate with the state of Bosnia, that is quite evident for very practical reasons. We must cooperate with the Bosnian authorities. If we did not cooperate, how could we manage, practically speaking? We have to have the Bosnian authorities as our interlocutors. That this be an exclusive legal obligation, an exclusive obligation to cooperate, that's something I'm not so sure about because we find ourselves in a very specific situation, a situation covered by Chapter VII. Chapter VII grants, in that particular case, the authority to the Security Council to decide, to reach a decision. So you cannot refer to the authority of the state, to the sovereignty of a state. The sovereignty becomes something that is peripheral to Chapter VII. In that particular case, there is priority given to Chapter VII that is stressed in Article 2(7), and the SFOR took action within that particular Article 2(7) and Chapter VII. That is the elements I wanted to introduce in this debate, because I don't think you've raised these different issues in your brief, Mr. Smith, and I did want to bring all this up to see what you had to say on the matter. I don't know if you have something to say on this, but, of course, I would like to hear from you if you have a particular opinion on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and I apologise if I have failed to make myself clear. I am not arguing that the Security Council could not have authorised enforcement methods that overrode national sovereignty under these provisions that Your Honour cites. I am arguing that they have not done so and that if they were to do so in the face of customary international law for dealing with these matters, it would have and should have been express and clear as a grant of authority because of the startling reach of the power that it would give the Prosecutor to conduct armed searches in Russia, for example, quite remarkable. I might mention several other things. The second sentence of Article 18, paragraph 2 that Judge Robinson mentioned seems to me to be required as appropriate, seek the assistance of state authorities language, because without authorisation, member states would have no requirement to respond to the Prosecutor, in particular. They need to know that the Prosecutor is authorised to request their assistance under Article 29. I would also mention that the Statute has been almost uniformly interpreted by the member states of the UN as involving the kind of judicial assistance for armed search and seizure that we are discussing here. There are 22 member states who have enacted special laws on cooperation with the ICTY and all regulate mutual assistance effectively in accordance with the international law bilateral, consensual model that Your Honour has mentioned. So I think that the views of the member states as well as the views that I cited earlier of the Tribunal itself, the Presidents of the Tribunal, all seem to be of one accord on this matter. But I hope I have cleared your question up. I am not arguing that the Security Council could not, if it had chosen, override under Article 7 the sovereignty of countries. They obviously can and do, and the current situation is an example. But on this point, I am arguing that given the breadth of the power being asserted here by the Prosecutor, they have not, and it would be a misinterpretation of their intent based on the slim language of on-site investigations and collecting evidence to conclude that they intended to allow armed intrusions in national territory for searches and seizures. I'm prepared at this point to turn to executions of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Smith, but maybe we can spend another minute on that particular issue. Article 18(2) of the Statute, you said that Judge Robinson quoted it, yes, indeed, he quoted it but only to inform you of the fact that the Prosecutor can ask, if necessary, the authorities of the relevant state to lend a helping hand. So, yes, the Prosecutor is authorised to collect evidence, and, yes, it is authorised to go into the country to execute those powers, but only for very practical reasons because the Prosecutor has no police force at its disposal. So the Prosecutor may, indeed, as appropriate seek the assistance of the state authorities concerned. Do you think that the Prosecutor cannot, for example, ask for the assistance of the SFOR, because this is what you're talking about basically. You are pushing us to reach the following conclusion. The Prosecutor, who is responsible pursuant to Article 18 to investigate and prepare the indictment has no police force of its own. It has to ask for the state's assistance. You are telling us that it cannot either seek the assistance of an international intervention force. Is that your argument, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Again, I fail to be clear enough, and I apologise. I am arguing that they could ask the assistance of SFOR to take actions which are within SFOR's jurisdiction, and we cited in our brief the SFOR power to support activities and to provide for security. SFOR does not, however, itself have the power to engage in an armed search and seizure. It may well have the power to arrest. It does not, it seems to me, have the power of search and seizure, and neither does the Prosecutor. In this case, neither of the two entities involved had the power to override sovereignty of the country of Bosnia. There is a distinction, I think, on the question of arrest in 59 bis. There is no equivalent to Rule 59 bis for purposes of search and seizure, even assuming that 59 bis doesn't expand improperly on the statutory authorities in the area of arrest. But that's not the issue in this case, nor is the refusal of the one state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to respect the arrest authority and extradition authority of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I wanted to go back to the question of mutual assistance treaties and the regime that governs those treaties. In those treaties, the standard formulation is that assistance, and certainly in the case of search and seizure, is to be carried out in accordance with the laws of the domestic state, of the state in which the search and seizure is carried out. Now, a state that enacts legislation to implement such a treaty would, of course, be entirely correct in enacting legislation that requires its consent or, at any rate, requires that the search and seizure be carried out in accordance with its laws. I've been trying to tell you that the situation here is different and for the reasons that Judge Bennouna and I have been trying to explain, the Chapter VII nature. If, for example, you look at Article 29 on cooperation and judicial assistance, Article 29 is itself a derogation from customary International Law. Under customary International Law, states cannot be obliged to cooperate in a judicial manner, particularly in relation to matters that affect them, affect their sovereignty, but Article 29, as the Blaskic judgement itself acknowledges, is a derogation from International Law. A state that enacts legislation, implement Article 29, cannot properly enact legislation that would require its consent for the implementation of Article 29, as one or two states have done, and as the Blaskic judgement itself, and I don't wish to name the states that have done that, but the Blaskic judgement itself says that that is quite improper. I mean, that legislation has no effect at all on the Tribunal in relation to Article 29. The fact that a state has enacted legislation that requires its consent for the implementation of Article 29 is totally irrelevant, because Article 29 delegates from customary International Law and the Blaskic judgement itself says so. So that I think what Judge Bennouna and I have been trying to explain to you is that the basis for action in this regard is entirely different from the basis for action in relation to the traditional judicial assistance treaty which proceeds on the basis of consensuality. Here it is the Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which imposes a certain regime and which overrides any treaty regime including even the treaty that you referred us to, by virtue of Article 103. I might say that when I pointed to the second sentence in Article 18(2), I think perhaps you interpreted it in the way that suited your ends. I was really trying to illustrate that what the Prosecutor is enabled to seek here is the assistance of the state and not the consent. He may seek the assistance. It does not say that he may seek the consent of the state. I mean, far less does it say that she must seek the consent of the state. It is assistance. It is cooperation, which is quite different from consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm arguing is that neither Article 18, nor Article 29 exercised in the Article 7 powers to require that states waive ipso facto their sovereign rights to object to armed search and seizure operations by the Office of the Prosecutor on their territory. If they had, if it were clear, if Article 18 had clearly granted that authority and Article 29 clearly reflected that the cooperation intended was that they waived their sovereignty, that would be a quite different case, but 22 countries have construed the cooperation obligations to allow them to grant consent, to withhold consent if they choose to, to require their consent before search and seizure operations are undertaken on their territories. That seems, to me, to be powerful evidence in the face of very little express language that goes to armed search and seizure in Article 18, that the framework is one in which that power was not exercised as to this sort of activity by the Security Council and that is, in effect, the argument that I've been trying to make, and I apologise if -- you are far more schooled than I in these issues involving bilateral treaties, but that is essentially the argument that I've been trying to make. It may be useful to quote the Blaskic case on this point, which we do at page 11. It says, "It is indubitable that states, being the addressees of the Article 29 Statute to cooperate, have some choice or leeway in identifying the persons responsible for and the method of its fulfilment. It is for each such state to determine the internal organs competent to carry out the order." It follows that if a Judge or a Chamber intends to order the production of documents, the seizure of evidence, the arrest of suspects, et cetera, being acts involving action by a state, its organs or officials, they must turn to the relevant state and the relevant state, in our judgement, would react under its special law on cooperation with the ICTY which provides, in the case of Bosnia, as in most states, for a mechanism similar, by analogy, to the normal judicial assistance mechanism in bilateral treaties which I understand are consensual. One of the points about a consensual bilateral treaty is that it can be consensual. A sovereign has no -- no one has the right, absent the consent of the sovereign, and, therefore, you have to have a treaty for the execution of a search warrant in another country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I recognise you haven't had the last hour and a half to yourself but, nonetheless, perhaps we can move on and try and complete your argument before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Let me do so quickly, Your Honour. The second basic argument in the case is the method of execution, and here we're dealing with the factual declarations by the Prosecutor and our affidavits. I would note, in dealing with that factual material first, that the three affidavits we have submitted are first-party material, that is to say, the person involved was present at the time in giving the material that he's describing. The Prosecution's declarations, two of them are not first party. Ms. Pantz was not at the locations of the inspection. She may have been in Sarajevo, but she was not at the locations of the inspection and she is reporting opinions, and legal conclusions, various other things that have been told to her. Dornan apparently, as near as we can determine, is the same thing. It is interesting that the person who was present at the inspection of the Zigonjic premises has not provided an affidavit. I would have normally thought there would be a first-party affidavit by that person that was present, but we note that it was not so. Issues we raise here, we have not raised the issue of probable cause, Your Honour, because as we indicated in our briefs at page 7 note 10, we cannot, not having been party to the issuance of the warrant, and indeed once we became aware that a search had taken place, we inquired of the defence council office whether we could obtain a copy of the search warrant and the materials leading up to it, and we were informed, after they had made inquiries, that those materials were not available to us. So we have not argued that because we could not. Secondly, a search warrant generally must have a concrete nexus among the places searched, the objects searched, and the alleged offences. This is a remarkably broad order with a number of people listed in the back of it, some of whom are currently in office, at least one of whom, I believe, is in office, and no real indication of the link between the people for whom information is sought and the particular crimes because there aren't any crimes actually stated on the face of the warrant. The Antunovic declaration shows that the Prosecutor is represented. He has seized virtually everything. In effect, a random search, and they simply took large volumes of material, some 44 boxes -- I think 45 boxes, perhaps, of material including hard disks and computer floppies that can contain a very large body of material in a very small space. As to the things seized, we note that weapons were seized and confiscated. They were not covered in the search warrant. We could understand their sequestration during the search, but it is not at all clear to us the legality of their confiscation and their retention the search was over. This was, of course, a defence office, and it was quite natural that one might find weapons at such a location. The inventory that was left was, in our judgement, too general. It was not in a language that could be understood by the person who had to sign it. There is some slight deviation in the accounts between our affidavits and the Prosecutor's declaration, but I remind Your Honours that ours is first party and except for the Antunovic search theirs is not on that point. We suggest without a detailed inventory, and none has been produce almost eight months later, this is a significant issue about the chain of custody and the validity of materials, and the owner can't tell what it was that has been taken in a case involving social security and welfare benefits for individuals. Finally, the materials, eight months on, have never been returned, nor has a copy been made even to return to those offices so they can proceed in their normal course of business. I suggest that this violates principles of International Law requiring the return of such materials when they are seized found in, for example, Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and there are similar provisions in the UN model convention on mutual assistance and the Commonwealth mutual assistance scheme. We believe that this was, in these regards, an improperly executed search and an illegally executed search, and that these materials should be, under Rule 95, excluded either on the grounds that they cast -- that the method of their acquisition, particularly given the broad inventory, the very general inventory, casts substantial doubt on the reliability of the evidence or, alternatively, that the method of the execution of the warrant and, in our judgement, the lack of the power to exercise an armed search and seizure operation without going through the requirements of Bosnian law is antithetical too or seriously damages the integrity of the proceedings were the Tribunal to allow this sort of evidence to be used by the Prosecutor. If the Tribunal is to control the exercise of investagatory powers by the Prosecutor so that they are lawful, we submit that the exclusion of evidence, generally the rule in most jurisdictions, is the effective tool for doing so. With, that Your Honour, I will conclude. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the usual break, quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't believe Mr. Kovacic wants to add anything. I'm not sure. Apparently not. I can deal with the points raised shortly. The potential for these powers contended for by the Prosecution to have been granted is conceded. We say they have been granted explicitly. The lack of complaint by the state in relation to this warrant, as, indeed, in relation to earlier warrants executed on its territory is not insignificant. It shows a recognition by the state of the legality of what's done, they neither seeking to arrest removal of materials by any domestic intervention, nor complaining, as they are entitled to, to this Tribunal under, I think, Rule 103. Dealing with a few of the points Mr. Smith raised and in the sequence in which he dealt with them, for the most part, non-cooperation has been dealt with just not in Ms. Pantz's affidavit but also extensively in the Prosecutor's brief at pages 9 and 10, where in the footnotes, there is reference to the annual reports to the Security Council which sets out extensively the history of non-cooperation. Mr. Smith relies today heavily, and I think more heavily than in the original motion, on the notion that this was an armed search. That is not the case, as is known, I'm sure, to the Court from its reading of the papers in this application. This was a search authorised by the warrant of the Court that SFOR attend, as they are obliged to do, to ensure the security of people whose presence on the territory they are aware of. It was their judgement and theirs alone what level of security was required. They took no part in the search. The example of the same powers being capable of exercise in France or the United States of America is worth perhaps the following four points: At the beginning, of course, when these powers were granted, the territory was in a state of war, and what's being contended for now might have been wholly inappropriate and would be completely different from what would apply in relation to a friendly and peaceful state. In any event, it may be, and it doesn't fall for determination today, but it may be that there is some limitation in the powers to affect search warrants in the phrase or words "on-site" in Article 18(2). But to deal, and it may be conclusively, with the problem, if there is any problem, in the example raised of France or the United States of America, the Prosecutor has in respect of search warrants always sought, as she can, an order of the Tribunal, and it may be that any application to exercise powers of search in respect of a country with which cooperation could be fully expected would be refused. Can I deal with the memorandum that was distributed? It, of course, in many ways is not in point at all. It is a memorandum about something entirely different and sets out quite a specific regime. But on page 10, paragraph 7, the Chamber may find something of interest where it says as follows, page 10, paragraph 7: "Investigators may take possession of documents and other pieces of physical evidence provided to them by witnesses during interviews, this is within the setting of the regime of interviews dealt with by this memorandum, but shall not exercise without a warrant or other order of a judge of the International Tribunal seek to exercise any powers of search or seizure," which all seem to acknowledge there and then the ability for such warrants to exercise such powers being granted. I turn from the memorandum just to make a couple of points about the Bosnian law referred to at page 17 of the defendant's motion, and it's their paragraph 32. As one of their witnesses first reveals and which has been possible for me to discover but only very recently, the citation is not as precise as the Chamber might have hoped for. In paragraph 32, there is reference to the Bosnian law on cooperation with the ICTY, and footnote 33 identifies the Statute of 1996. That Statute is apparently and exclusively a statute on the laws of extradition. It is not a statute headed and titled, as I am informed but I'm afraid only now informed today, on cooperation. When it goes on to say that Article 27 requires any final order to collect evidence should be executed by the Ministry of Justice and administration and so on, the position is that Article 27 refers to the regime appropriate to the return of somebody being extradited and Article 28 makes a reference to the production or collection of property and says that the regime for that material must be the same as Article 27. Finally, when it is said that Article 6 of the law of cooperation explicitly designates the code of procedure as the law that regulates the judicial assistance procedures, my understanding is that the code of criminal procedure is invoked as a residuary code to be applied where things are not otherwise specified but this all in a statute that deals with extradition. So that whatever value it is that may be diminished by its precise terms, in any event, as I think has been made plain, unilateral laws are not to the point if, as we contend, quite explicit powers of the type required have been given to this Office of the Prosecutor by the Statute. I think that we've set out at our page 7 a relevant quotation from the Blaskic decision which sets out how on-site activity may require to be done unilaterally and without notice, and that fits entirely with the reasoning that lies behind the powers that we say are granted. So far as Article 18 and Article 29 are concerned, we say that this matter is governed by Article 18. I needn't repeat the section and further identify the distinction between the first and second sentence. Article 29 deals with cooperation. This was not a question of seeking and obtaining acts by cooperation. It's true that notice was given simultaneously with execution of the warrants, and so it could be said that at that stage and from that moment, cooperation was required and was granted, but we rely on the quite clear and precise terms of Article 18. I turn briefly to deal with the matters of fact. I've explained to Mr. Smith, and I'm sure he accepts, the only reason why the affidavits produced do not include an affidavit from the investigator who dealt with the particular site and who read the correct but left the wrong warrant is because he's the investigator who sadly died earlier this year, having contacted, I think, a tropical disease in the course of the winter. That's the only reason that you don't have the first-hand affidavit. This warrant and its breadth reflect the fact that it was not, of course, solely restricted to an investigation into these two defendants. This was wider than that. So far as weapons seized were concerned, that was entirely a matter for SFOR. It had nothing to do with the search warrant, and as I understand it, SFOR, in different locations, may have made different judgements in relation to weapons that they discovered were found. But it was a matter for them and had nothing to do with the search warrant. The material sought was wide and, of course, its breadth was approved by the Court when the warrant was granted, and there's no challenge to the appropriateness of the Court making the decision it did on the material available to it. The inventory preparation was necessarily an extensive exercise. Statistics revealing how extensive are, I think, contained on the last page of Ms. Pantz's affidavit. The Defence were provided on the 1st of April with an extract from the full inventory still then in the process of preparation, and the extract of some 88 pages related to documents identified as particularly appropriate or potentially appropriate to the defendants. The process of completing the inventories continued, and the full inventories were sent out not to the defendants but to the custodians on the 14th of May of this year. Some have, as I understand it, and some have not yet reached the final custodians, it being an administrative matter to make sure they find the right office or person. In summary, we say, as we said in the motion and have nothing much further to add, nothing further to add, the powers were explicitly envisaged and given. This warrant was correctly granted. Its execution, as revealed by the material, the evidential material before you, was entirely proper, and there is no grounds here whatsoever for excluding admission of any of this evidence on the grounds that it was obtained pursuant to the search warrant. I can simply add that material from the search warrants has already been admitted in other cases. Before entering premises, it would not be possible to know the quantity of potentially useful material that might be revealed, but it was possible to forecast and SFOR so forecast, as it were, that there would only be the potential for one day's work. So everything had to be accommodated within one day. Any overnight pause was unacceptable -- sorry, overnight continuation was not possible, so far as SFOR was concerned, and a pause overnight would render the following day's exercise potentially valueless. It all had to be dealt with in one day. That explains the hierarchy of inventories that had to be prepared. It simply wouldn't be possible to prepare a detailed inventory of the amount of material that was, in the event, found to be of potential value, given the resources and the time available. Of course, surprise was necessary, though I don't think it's dealt with specifically in the evidence. One can give examples within these very searches, not necessarily this particular one that concerns Mr. Smith, but searches on the same day are the sort of events that can happen at computers if there is any advance notice given that a search is going to take place. I return briefly to the legal argument that has been advanced in relation to the granting of an exercise of warrants generally. If the Defence argument is right, then even assuming ground forces enter Kosovo while it remains part of Serbia, it would not be lawful for any force of the Office of the Prosecutor following the armed forces to search premises for documents, because they would still have to operate through the state. With great respect, that simply isn't right. These powers were granted to deal with a particular known situation. They have been properly exercised, and, in our respectful submission, the evidence should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I will be quite brief, Your Honour. First, the citation of the statement by Louise Arbour which is comparing her powers to those that the Nuremberg Tribunal had: "They ruled over the territory. I can only imagine how quickly we would finish in the former Yugoslavia if we could enter any ministry and take documents that we need." That is on page 4, footnote 2 of our motion for advance notice. That's the first matter. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me find that. Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Page 4, footnote 2 of the second set of briefs relating to this matter, that is, relating to the motion for advance notice of the Prosecutor's intent to offer evidence, dated 8 March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's presumably a purely factual comment, comparing the position at Nuremberg with the position here. It's not any comment about the powers or legality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I had read it and taken it as having an implicit predicate which was that she could not enter any Ministry and take any documents, and if she could she would. I may be incorrect on that matter, Your Honours. That's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a pure matter of fact, it's not a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the question of lack of complaint, I've addressed that already. That's not at issue. It's lack of consent that is at question. But on that point and the question of whether this was an armed search, I think that the affidavits we have submitted leave no doubt. SFOR was present for security purposes, but the search warrant, in paragraph 8, expressly authorised the use of force and that was handed to the persons at the search site. In the paragraphs of the affidavits, Mr. Zigonjic, Mr. Antunovic both indicate that the presence of the armed troops made them afraid to resist. It was clearly under threat of force and that when they checked up the line of authority, they were told that they had no choice but not to oppose the search. I can, if you like, take the time to point out the particular paragraphs, otherwise, I will simply leave Your Honours to see the testimony by the persons against whom the threat of force in the search and seizure was applied. Indeed, the Minister -- Your Honours indicated earlier that he was now the Minister. He is not. He is the former Minister of Justice. In paragraph 6 of his affidavit, he says, "I contacted the Ministry of Defence to see what course to take. They said that they had also been visited by the representatives of the Prosecutor and were given warrants. They were also surprised by such act because the SFOR was armed and had deployed armoured vehicles. We," the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Defence, in other words, "decided not to react in order to avoid shooting. On top of that, there was no point in our resisting the execution of the search as it had already been commenced." Indeed, the seizure of the weapons indicates that SFOR disarmed the persons being searched. I think it is not possible to call this anything but an armed search and seizure. If the U.S. Prosecutor went into a location with the aid of police that, it seems to me, under threat of force, is, in effect, exactly what has happened here. On the question whether this power could be or would be asserted against the U.S., or Russia, or France, or any other major power, I think the suggestion was made that the U.S. Would simply refuse but that is not the issue here. The power asserted, they would have no opportunity to refuse. What is asserted is the unilateral power without advance notice or consultation by armed force to seize evidence anywhere in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, or Russia, and I suggest to Your Honours that those countries would be startled, as would China, for example, to find that power asserted by the Prosecutor even subject to a search warrant. A search warrant was issued here. It is the execution of the search warrant without the consent of the sovereign nation which is at fault, not the search warrant itself. The search warrant perfectly was, in that regard in terms of power, properly issued. I'm the not conceding probable cause or any of the specifics, but the point is it is the execution unilaterally in a sovereign country that we believe is clearly not authorised by the Statute. On the memorandum of understanding, the Prosecutor has cited the provision dealing with evidence, as he properly indicates, supplied by a witness during an interview. First of all, that is not what has evolved here. This is in a section of the memorandum of understanding that deals with witnesses. That is not the situation. In any case, that language notes that even with a warrant, the Prosecutor must seek to exercise, he must go and request consent under the laws relating to cooperation with the Tribunal. Seek to exercise. Furthermore, in that same section dealing with witnesses, in paragraph 5 it provides that investigators will not be armed. This is just a provision which is not applicable in this situation. On the question of the Blaskic opinion, we have read to Your Honours the language dealing with search and seizure. That is the relevant language, not language dealing with on-site activity, as the Prosecutor terms it. As to the statistics in the declaration by Ms. Pantz, the statistics are 45 boxes, formats with large acetate coverings, as I recall. On the question of question of the inventories and the return of the materials, I suggest to Your Honours that whatever may be the difficulties in providing a detailed inventory, which has now apparently been provided eight months on, there simply is no excuse for not copying 45 boxes of materials and returning the originals to the office so that the persons whose social security benefits and other benefits could be provided by the office and its activities are not brought to a halt. If you will look at the affidavits by Zigonjic and Antunovic, you will see that they both say that having the material taken away from them, and even now, even with the inventory provided, no copy apparently, no original back to the working office in charge of social security benefits for individuals just seems to us to be unlikely to be well-received by the persons in the country in question. Finally on the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down a bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. On the question of the powers in Kosovo, I am by no means an expert on the laws of conflict, but I suggest to Your Honours that if NATO occupies Kosovo, the power to -- and does so under Article 7, enforcement powers, that it becomes, in the effect, in some sense an occupying power, and if the Prosecutor looked carefully at the law, he would find that he did not require the consent of the Yugoslav government or the Serbian government, particularly when it is that government which has, in the context of Rule 59 bis, clearly enacted legislation to prohibit exercise of powers by this Tribunal. That is not the case in the situation that we're dealing with or would be the case in any other country -- virtually any other country, particularly the 22 that have enacted these statutes, laws, dealing with cooperation with the Tribunal. Because I can't read the Croatian, I request Your Honours leave to have my colleague, Ms. Turkovic, dealing with the provisions in the 1996 law and the code of procedure that the Prosecutor was citing. If she could be allowed to do that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is true, as the Prosecutor has asserted, that the title of the law is, and I will read in Croatian so that the interpreter can interpret, not myself in English, (As read) (Interpretation) "Decree on the proclamation of the law on extraditing criminals accused, at the demand of the International Tribunal." (In English) However, the title in section 3 is: (Interpretation) "Extraditing individuals and objects, handing over." (In English) And I will read Article 27: (As read) (Interpretation) "A decision to hand over, based on the law, be executed by the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina in cooperation with the Ministry for Internal Affairs of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs according to the rule regulating the handing over of individuals and objects which together be brought by the competent Ministers. "These rules and regulations shall be enacted within 15 days from the day that they come into being, become effective, from the day this law becomes effective." Article 28.1 states that: (As read) "Objects for which or with the help of which a criminal act has been committed or objects which can serve as evidence and are requested by the International Tribunal shall be handed over to the International Tribunal in keeping with the rules from Article 27 of this law." (In English) I have to point out that these rules have never been enacted. Maybe you know it's really difficult in Bosnia today to actually obtain the consent and to enact quite a number of the laws, especially those that are sensitive and related to the ICTY. As related to the Criminal Code, I will just read the title of the section which is: (As read) (Interpretation) "Proceedings for Giving International Legal Assistance." (In English) So it's not extradition, it's legal assistance, and Article 518, which says: (As read) (Interpretation) "Requests by domestic courts for legal assistance in criminal proceedings shall be sent follows." (In English) Throughout the whole Article and Article 519 they talk about (Interpretation) "International legal assistance." We can provide the Articles if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: To conclude, Your Honour, this is, as I believe Your Honours appreciate, a matter of grave consequence to powers asserted by the Prosecutor in this situation, and that is why the Defence has raised the matter. I think I indicated at a proceeding some time ago the seriousness with which the Defence viewed the nature of the search and seizure operation and the way it was conducted. We submit that these powers, as exercised by the Prosecutor, are not granted by the Statute, are not covered by the Rules, are, therefore, unlawful and were improperly executed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why would one -- one final point, Mr. Smith. Even if you were right about your submissions, you would also have to show that the admission would cast doubt on the reliability of the evidence, and that is documentary evidence, remember, or to admit it would be antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Now, the proceedings must mean the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, why would it seriously damage the integrity of the trial if we admitted this evidence, even if we accepted your earlier argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, for a very fundamental reason, and that is that if the behaviour is lawless, if it is beyond the legal power of the Prosecutor, this Tribunal cannot, in our judgement, and should not be party to the use of that evidence. It is morally incongruous for the Tribunal both to argue that criminals tried before it should have obeyed the law but that the Prosecutor need not. Point number one. Point number two, respect for the rule of law, in our judgement, demands that the evidence be excluded. Third, the fairness of the system is fundamentally dependent on lawful behaviour by the Prosecutor. The legitimacy of the verdict is of very great importance, and a verdict based on evidence admitted which was unlawfully seized, seized outside the power of the Prosecutor, would, it seems to me, be seen in many quarters as an illegitimate verdict. Finally and most fundamentally, the ends simply do not and cannot justify the means. This court needs power to operate effectively.
