I have no doubt of that, but it's our submission that it cannot be seen, particularly at this embryonic stage in its development and at a time at which it is taking indictments of major international significance and attracting attention to itself, it simply seems to us that it must, it must provide for the exclusion of illegally seized evidence and call the shots as they may fall. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I really wanted to ask you how you respond to Mr. Smith's contention that in a matter of this kind one would expect to find an explicit provision in either the Statute or the Rules providing for search and seizure. He says there is no such explicit provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We answer that quite simply by saying this is both explicit provision and the explicit delegated but effectively delegated power for the Judges to make further provision. 18(2) is wide enough and does cover exactly what happened. I repeat -- I don't repeat, because I never set it out. Taking it as read: "To collect evidence and to conduct on-site investigations." The court will also have in mind Article 19(2) that: "Upon confirmation of an indictment the Judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issue such orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, and surrender," and so on, as may be required for the conduct of the trial. Whether or not that further amplifies the position, Article 18(2), in our respectful submission, is quite explicit. Article 54 may also be worth consideration. Rule 54, I beg your pardon. Rule 54 again we've referred to. It's quite broad, and intentionally so: "At the request of either party or of its own motion the Judge may issue orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants, and transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of an investigation or the preparation or conduct of the trial." There can be no doubt, in the setting of this history and this Tribunal, that these powers are necessary. They're not optional. They are absolutely necessary. The Chamber must be under no illusions in light of its comparatively recent encounters in this case with the need for documentary material, the difficulties of obtaining it, whether by cooperation or otherwise, and thus its dependence on the search warrant provision, a provision that has been executed already, as I say, unchallenged on several occasions. But my answer remains that it is allowed for. It may not be spelt out in the words "search warrant," but it is allowed for by specific provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Less than that, Your Honour. Rule 54 authorises a Judge or a Trial Chamber to issue an order, and that is not a question here. There was a search warrant issued. The problem is that it was improperly executed in a way that the Prosecutor had no power to do, a unilateral execution without going through the provisions of the law of the state which is sovereign and on whose territory it was executed, and that is not required by the search warrant itself. There is nothing in the four squares of the search warrant that authorises that or that purported to authorise it. The Trial Chamber and the Judge issuing it did not face that issue when he issued it. It was the steps taken by the Prosecutor subsequently. Rule 54 is of no assistance on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, part of what Mr. Smith has said you have not answered to, the part dealing with the possibility of returning some of the documents which were seized by you within the framework of that warrant, search warrant. Can you answer that part of his argument, that possibility of returning some of the documents which were seized?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two answers. First of all, I doubt with whether, as a matter of principle, what happens after a lawfully executed search warrant is executed can render the execution itself unlawful, and the remedy of an offended party would be either directly to the Chamber for relief, or if the party were a defendant at trial, an argument objecting to the admissibility of the evidence. In this case, we know not only that there has been no official complaint from the government about the execution of the search warrant, but save for the statement in an unofficial capacity of a former office holder, no complaint of any kind. So that as a matter of law or mixed law and fact as it affects your decision on this application, I would respectfully say it has no effect. Second part of the answer, a practical one, the decision about preparing inventories and returning material is not one directly within the power of the lawyers in the Office of the Prosecutor. As I have already explained, this material was sought not just for this trial and, therefore, the decision as to when it should be returned falls to those who have a wider brief than the lawyers in just this trial. Having said that, no doubt, now that the full process of preparing inventories has been completed, decisions about return of material can and presumably will be made, but it seems to me that that is a practical matter as opposed to one that really affects your decision here today or whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would simply refer Your Honours to Article 7 of the UN model treaty on mutual assistance in criminal matters, which deals with return of material to the requested state and states: "Any property, as well as original records or documents handed over to the requesting state under the present treaty, shall be returned to the requested state as soon as possible unless the latter waives its right of return thereof." I suggest to you that that is the accepted international practice, and it's no answer to say that it has not been complied with and there is no remedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will take these matters under consideration. We will announce a decision in due course. We will adjourn now until tomorrow, half past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 5.35 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of June, 1999 at 2:30 p.m. 24 25
